summary: Defines a simple application-layer protocol that lets remote users inspect or change management information on a gateway. It was an interim answer to immediate gateway monitoring needs. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: It is a basic way to look at a router's dials from far away and turn a few knobs, before better tools came along.

subtitle: An early way to monitor and manage Internet routers from afar.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed a way to inspect and change settings on Internet routers from a remote location, but existing tools were not standardized or portable across different router vendors.
tldr.mechanism: SGMP defines a simple client-server protocol where managers send Get and Set requests to retrieve or change named variables on a gateway, plus Trap messages from gateways to alert managers of problems like link failures.
tldr.outcome: SGMP was intentionally a temporary solution while more comprehensive management systems were being developed. It evolved into SNMP (RFC 1157), which became the standard for network management and remains in use today.

today: RFC 1028 is Historic. SGMP was succeeded by the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP, RFC 1157), which uses the same basic model of reading and writing named variables but adds a hierarchical variable naming scheme and became the standard for network management. SNMP remains the dominant protocol for monitoring and managing IP networks.

sections.title: A Simple Gateway Monitoring System
sections.content:
RFC 1028 defines the Simple Gateway Monitoring Protocol (SGMP), an application-layer protocol that allows administrators to inspect and alter management information on Internet routers from a remote host. Written in 1987 by researchers at several universities and Proteon, Inc., SGMP was intended as a quick, interim solution to an immediate need for gateway monitoring while more elaborate and robust systems were being designed.

The protocol is deliberately simple: the gateway keeps a set of named variables (such as the number of packets received on an interface, or the version of its software), and a remote manager can request their values or set them. The design philosophy emphasizes simplicity on the gateway side at the expense of complexity on the management tools.
sections.eli5: A network manager can ask a router "How many packets came in?" or "Change this setting," and the router answers with the information or makes the change. It is like a phone line that lets you read and set dials on a machine in another building.

sections.title: Design Philosophy and Goals
sections.content:
SGMP was designed around seven key principles. First, the protocol minimizes the number and complexity of functions realized by the gateway itself, reducing development cost and keeping gateways simple. Second, it is extensible, allowing managers to monitor or control new variables as needs arise. Third, it is independent of the architecture of any particular host or gateway, promoting vendor interoperability.

Fourth, all gateway management is modeled as alterations or inspections of parameter values (variables)—rather than issuing imperative commands—which simplifies both the protocol and implementations. Fifth, the protocol adopts X.409 encoding conventions, providing machine-independent data representation. Sixth, variables assume only integer or octet string types to keep parsing simple. Seventh, every protocol message is represented by a single unreliable UDP datagram, minimizing transport overhead.
sections.eli5: The designers wanted to keep the router as simple as possible, make it easy to add new things to monitor, and use simple variable names instead of complex commands.

sections.title: Messages, Variables and Traps
sections.content:
SGMP defines four message types. Get Request messages ask for the value of variables on the gateway; the gateway responds with Get Response messages containing the names and values. Set Request messages ask the gateway to change variables; the gateway confirms with a Get Response. Trap Request messages are sent by the gateway to alert managers of noteworthy events: Cold Start (gateway rebooting, configuration may change), Warm Start (gateway restarting without changing configuration), Link Failure (a communication link is down), Authentication Failure (a message was not properly authenticated), or EGP Neighbor Loss (an external gateway peer went down).

Variables are named with octet strings (octets of binary data), and variable names are chosen so that related variables are consecutive in lexicographic order, allowing sequential access to groups of related variables. The protocol includes required variables such as gateway version identification, the number of network interfaces, and for each interface, its type, speed, packet counts, byte counts, error counts and status. Additional variables track IP routing information (addresses, routes, metrics) and EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) peer state.
sections.eli5: A manager asks for a variable's value, or tells the gateway to change one. The gateway can also send a message saying "Something important happened." All the things the gateway tracks have names so the manager can ask for any of them.

sections.title: Authentication and Access Control
sections.content:
SGMP separates authentication from the main monitoring protocol. An underlying authentication protocol layer validates that incoming messages are authentic and authorizes the manager to access certain variables. The initial implementation uses trivial authentication—every message is accepted as authentic—but the design allows for more sophisticated authentication mechanisms to be plugged in later.

Access control is managed through the association between management sessions and instances of the protocol entity. Different managers may be granted different access levels: some may have Read-Only access (to inspect variables but not change them), while others have Read-Write access. The specification does not mandate specific variable definitions for authentication; implementations are free to add security features as needed. The protocol operates on UDP port 153 and encodes messages in the X.409 format.
sections.eli5: The protocol includes a slot for an authentication system to verify that the person asking really is allowed to look at or change things. Different managers can have different permissions.

sections.title: A Bridge to SNMP
sections.content:
The RFC explicitly states that SGMP is an interim solution. The authors note that initial implementations might not support Set Request messages at all, and that the authentication mechanism is simplified for quick deployment. They urge implementors to design with extensibility in mind, isolating the authentication layer so that better security can be added later.

SGMP quickly led to the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP, RFC 1157), which adopted SGMP's core approach of reading and writing named variables but added a more structured variable naming scheme (the SNMP MIB, Management Information Base). SNMP became the foundation of network management standards and remains the primary protocol for managing IP networks today.
sections.eli5: The inventors said this was temporary, a quick fix to solve the immediate problem while they thought about better ways. Within a few years, SNMP (its successor) became the real standard for managing routers.
